## The Setting, You'll Recall

- The setting for *unsupervised learning* is that you have:

  + a collection of $p$ measurements (recorded in columns of a data frame),
  
  + for each of $n$ objects (recorded in rows of a data frame)
  
- "Unsupervised" simply means that none of the variables is a response variable: we are not trying to predict the value of a measurement

- One can think of unsupervised learning as being an extension of EDA

  + in EDA, the goal is to visualize *projected* data to build intuition and to visually assess potential associations between variables
  
  + in unsupervised learning, we implement statistical algorithms to uncover potential structure in the data in their native space, i.e., quantitatively accounting for those potential associations between variables

- A main, overarching issue with unsupervised learning is that *there are no universally accepted mechanisms for model assessment or selection, i.e., there will almost never be a uniquely correct answer!*


---

## Hierarchical Clustering

- The algorithm for hierarchical clustering is, like that for $k$-means, straightforward:

.center[
  ![:scale 50%](./alg_10-2.png)
]

- Note the sentence: "Treat each observation as its own cluster." 

  + this is "bottom-up" or *agglomerative* clustering
  
  + a primary limitation of agglomerative clustering is that all clusters lie within other clusters (hence the name "hierarchical")


---

## Hierarchical Clustering: Example

- Here's an example of that *dendrogram* referenced for *complete-linkage hierarchical clustering*

  + the "height" along the vertical axis at which two clusters fuse indicates their dissimilarity $-$ the greater the vertical height of a merge point, the greater the dissimilarity between the merged clusters
  
```{r echo=FALSE}
set.seed(101)
x  <- c(rnorm(30), rnorm(30, mean = 2.25))
y  <- c(rnorm(30), rnorm(30, mean = 2.25))
s  <- c(rep(2, 30), rep(19, 30))
df <- data.frame(x, y)
```

```{r fig.height=4.5,fig.width=4.5,fig.align="center"}
hc.out <- hclust(dist(scale(df)), method = "complete")   # we use the same data as we did for k-means
plot(hc.out)
```

## Hierarchical Clustering: Linkage

- In agglomerative clustering, clusters are built up piece-by-piece by *linking* them together

  + there is no uniquely correct algorithm for how that linking is done
  
  + commonly used methods are single, complete, and average linkage

<br>

.center[
  ![:scale 45%](./linkage.png)
]

## Hierarchical Clustering: the Elbow Method

```{r warning=FALSE,fig.height=4.5,fig.width=4.5,fig.align="center"}
suppressMessages(library(factoextra))
fviz_nbclust(scale(df), FUN = hcut, method = "wss")
```

- Note that in the examples shown in *this* set of slides, we'll exclusively use functions from the `factoextra` package.

## Hierarchical Clustering: the Gap Statistic

```{r warning=FALSE,fig.height=4.5,fig.width=4.5,fig.align="center"}
library(cluster)
gs <- clusGap(scale(df), FUN = hcut, nstart = 20, K.max = 10, B = 50)
fviz_gap_stat(gs)
```

## K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering: Wrap-Up

- So: which of these options should you use?

- Quoting *ISLR*: 

  + "we recommend performing clustering with different choices of [methods and parameters], and looking at the full set of results in order to see what patterns consistently emerge"

- That said:

  + in $k$-means, you specify the number of clusters before running the algorithm, as opposed to hierarchical clustering, where you specify the number of clusters afterwards by cutting the a dendrogram

  + dendrograms can be *really* hard to read when the sample size is large

  + all data get assigned to a cluster in these algorithms


---

## About That Last Point...

- Perhaps we would like to implement an algorithm that does not necessarily force every datum into a cluster

  + one example of such an algorithm is the [Gaussian Mixture Model](http://www.ee.iisc.ac.in/new/people/faculty/prasantg/downloads/GMM_Tutorial_Reynolds.pdf)

<br>

.center[
  ![:scale 30%](./gmm.png)
]

<br>

([Courtesy this web page](https://www.python-course.eu/expectation_maximization_and_gaussian_mixture_models.php))


---

## GMM: Example

- Here we will use the `ClusterR` package to determine the probabilities that data belong to one of a pre-defined number of Gaussian-shaped clusters

  + a limitation of this model is that the Gaussians are *diagonal*: the longest axis lies along the $x$ or $y$ axis, and is not allowed to rotate away from those axes

<br><br>

.center[
  ![:scale 80%](./gmm2.png)
]


---

## GMM: Example

```{r warning=FALSE}
suppressMessages(library(ClusterR))
gmm.out <- GMM(df, gaussian_comps = 2)
pred    <- predict_GMM(df, gmm.out$centroids, gmm.out$covariance_matrices, gmm.out$weights)
gmm.out$centroids
names(pred)
```

- In this output:

  + `log_likelihood` is the natural logarithm of the probability density function values at each data point

  + `cluster_proba` is a matrix of probabilities: each row represents a data point, and each column the probability that the data point is in that cluster

  + `cluster_labels` is the predicted cluster; it's the identity of which column had the highest probability for that data point


---

## GMM: Example

- Our simulated data were drawn from two normal distributions, thus we might expect to see that they map to one of the two normals under the GMM with high probability

  + the plot below shows the probability of each data point belonging to *cluster 1*
  
<br>
  
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.height=4.5,fig.width=4.5,fig.align="center"}
suppressMessages(library(tidyverse))
df <- data.frame("p" = pred$cluster_proba[, 1])
ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = p, y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "mediumorchid")
```
